name: Review a Paper
description: Critical review of methodology, statistical rigor, limitations, and constructive feedback
prompt:
Prepare an evidence-bounded peer-review draft of the supplied paper. Treat unpublished material as confidential and settle intake and safety requirements before analysis: if authorization to use AI, the venue's AI/confidentiality policy, a conflict of interest, or the requested review scope is unclear, ask only the minimum blocking questions together via the interview tool before reading or quoting the manuscript. Do not expose confidential manuscript text or distinctive details to web searches or other external services.

Work in this order:
1. Establish the review context, materials available, intended scope, and any competence limits. If no special focus is requested, perform a comprehensive review.
2. Give a short, neutral study map: research question, design, population or system, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes, and principal claims. Distinguish information that is not reported from information that is methodologically inadequate.
3. Assess claim-evidence alignment. For each central claim, identify the supporting result, figure, table, or analysis and judge whether the direction, magnitude, uncertainty, population, and causal language are supported.
4. Evaluate study design and methods: sampling, controls, randomization or masking where applicable, unit of analysis, confounding and bias, measurement validity, sample-size or precision rationale, missing data, and fit to the relevant reporting guideline.
5. Evaluate statistics: test-model fit, assumptions, multiplicity and prespecification, effect sizes, confidence or credible intervals, exact denominators, robustness or sensitivity analyses, and whether interpretation exceeds the design.
6. Review reproducibility and transparency, including protocol or registration consistency, data and code availability, software and parameter reporting, ethics approvals, consent, funding, conflicts, and contribution statements where applicable.
7. Check every figure, table, and citation that bears on a central conclusion for consistency with the text, readable labeling, denominators, units, uncertainty, and adequate context.
8. Draft the review as: review scope and limits; concise summary; key strengths; major comments; minor comments; and an overall evidence assessment. Each comment must include the manuscript location, the observation, why it matters, and a specific proportionate action. Prioritize threats to validity and claim support over stylistic preferences. Do not recommend acceptance or rejection unless the user explicitly requests it and the venue permits it; keep any confidential editor-only comments separate from comments to authors.

Ground every statement in the supplied materials and cite exact section, page, figure, table, or line locations when available. Never invent quotations, data, analyses, citations, manuscript locations, or author intentions. State uncertainty, flag specialist-review needs, and avoid requesting new experiments unless they are necessary to support a central claim; suggest clarification, reanalysis, narrower claims, or added limitation language when sufficient. Label the result as a working draft requiring human verification. Save it as a clearly named Markdown file in the sandbox, then give a brief chat summary of the most consequential strengths, concerns, unresolved questions, and saved path.

1. Establish schema, units, identifiers, independent units, study design and intended analysis. Inspect size first; use bounded/chunked inspection when necessary and distinguish sampled checks from exact totals.
2. Profile types, missingness, duplicates and plausible ranges against domain rules. Repeated observations are not automatically duplicates, and extreme values are not automatically errors.
3. Propose the minimum justified transformations. Do not drop, impute, winsorize, scale or encode by default; explain each needed choice, retain raw inputs and record affected row/cell counts. Ask only about ambiguities that materially change interpretation.
4. For predictive work, establish group/time-aware train/validation/test separation before learning imputation, scaling, encoding or outlier thresholds. Fit these operations on training folds only and apply the fitted transformations to held-out data. For inference, choose missing-data handling compatible with the model and assumptions.
5. Write cleaned data separately with a reproducible transformation script and a before/after validation report, preserving identifiers and a change log. State unresolved issues and any inspection limits. Save outputs in the sandbox and name their paths.

name: Build a Predictive Model
description: Train and evaluate ML models on supplied data
prompt:
Build a predictive model on the supplied data. Target variable: {target}. If the task type (regression vs classification) or evaluation metric is ambiguous and would change results, ask the minimum set of blocking questions together via the interview tool; otherwise state assumptions.

Work in this order:
1. Explore data, check missingness, class balance, and screen for leakage.
2. Make a train/validation/test split (or nested CV) and fit preprocessing inside the pipeline to prevent leakage.
3. Establish a simple baseline, then train appropriate models, tuning only on validation/CV.
4. Evaluate on the held-out test set with task-appropriate metrics (accuracy, AUC, F1, RMSE, MAE) plus uncertainty and calibration where relevant.
5. Interpret with SHAP/feature importance.
6. Set and report a random seed and key package versions. Deliverables: save the trained model, predictions CSV, figures PNG, and a Markdown report to the sandbox; summarize in chat, name files, and state limitations.

name: Time Series Analysis
description: Trend decomposition, forecasting, and anomaly detection
prompt:
Analyze and, when requested, forecast the supplied time series. Requested forecast horizon: {horizon}.

1. Establish the time index/frequency, timezone, target, forecast horizon, decision-time availability of predictors, and whether there are multiple entities or irregular observations. Inspect gaps, duplicates, changes in measurement and relevant seasonality; do not impute or aggregate without a justified rule.
2. Plot and characterize trend, seasonality and residual dependence. Use stationarity diagnostics only where the candidate model requires them; do not mechanically difference every series or treat ADF/KPSS as universal method selectors.
3. For forecasting, reserve an untouched final chronological test window covering the intended horizon. Compare simple/seasonal baselines and suitable models with rolling/expanding-origin validation on earlier data. Respect entity dependence and label availability; add a gap when needed to prevent overlap leakage.
4. Fit preprocessing, imputation, transformations and model selection within each training window using only information available at that origin. Tune on validation windows only; evaluate the selected procedure once on the final test. If history is insufficient, report that limitation instead of silently reusing the test for tuning.
5. Report horizon-specific errors with appropriate metrics (for example MAE/RMSE; avoid MAPE with zero or near-zero targets), uncertainty/coverage and interval assumptions. Separate validation backtests, final test results and future forecasts. A model refit on all observed data for deployment has not been evaluated on an untouched future sample.
6. For descriptive analysis without a forecasting request, omit model tuning and future forecasts unless needed for the question. Save reproducible code, plots, tables and a Markdown report in the sandbox, documenting versions, seeds where used, assumptions and limitations.

name: Survival Analysis
description: Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox regression, and hazard modeling
prompt:
Perform survival analysis on the supplied data. First verify the time and event (censoring) columns and check follow-up and censoring patterns.

Work in this order:
1. Generate Kaplan-Meier curves with confidence bands for key groups and report median survival.
2. Run log-rank tests for group comparisons.
3. Fit a Cox proportional hazards model with covariates: {covariates}, checking multicollinearity and screening for leakage.
4. Test the proportional hazards assumption (Schoenfeld residuals) and address violations if found.
5. Report hazard ratios with 95% CIs and p-values, plus model fit (concordance).
6. Create forest plots. Set and report a random seed and key package versions. Deliverables: save figures as PNG, a results table as CSV, and a Markdown report to the sandbox; summarize in chat, name files, and state limitations.

name: Meta-Analysis
description: Pool effect sizes across studies with heterogeneity assessment
prompt:
Synthesize the supplied study data with a design-appropriate meta-analysis.

1. Define the question, eligibility criteria, outcome, effect metric/direction and unit of synthesis. Verify effect sizes and sampling variances; identify overlapping cohorts, multi-arm studies and multiple effects from the same study before assuming independence. Document exclusions and missing information.
2. Choose a primary fixed-effect or random-effects model from the estimand and scientific assumptions, not a heterogeneity-test threshold. If comparing both, label the second as sensitivity analysis. Explain the heterogeneity estimator and interval method; account for dependent effects when present. Report the pooled effect with uncertainty. Provide a prediction interval only for a suitable random-effects model and qualify sparse-study uncertainty.
3. Assess and interpret heterogeneity (tau-squared, I-squared and Q as appropriate), alongside clinical/design differences and the precision of these estimates. Generate a forest plot with correctly interpreted weights.
4. Assess missing-evidence risk using protocols, registrations and reporting information when available. Consider funnel plots/asymmetry tests only when applicable: usually at least 10 studies, sufficient variation in standard errors and a test appropriate to the effect metric. Do not automatically run the original Egger test for odds ratios or standardized mean differences. With too few studies, report limited assessment rather than absence of bias. Asymmetry has multiple explanations and does not establish publication bias.
5. Run justified influence/sensitivity analyses. Perform subgroup/meta-regression only with sufficient information and a rationale; distinguish prespecified from exploratory analyses and avoid searching for significance.
6. Save plots, study-level/pooled-result tables and a Markdown report in the sandbox. Record data sources, model choices, package versions, seeds where used and limitations; state when pooling is not defensible.

name: Power Analysis

prompt:
Perform an a priori power and sample-size analysis for a {study_design}. Use expected effect size = {effect_size} and significance level = {alpha} (default 0.05 if unspecified). Do not invent an effect size or report post-hoc observed power; if the study is already complete, report the minimum detectable effect at the achieved sample size instead.

Work in this order:
1. Define the independent unit, allocation, primary endpoint, hypotheses, planned analysis, sidedness, and effect-size metric.
2. Justify a plausible effect-size range, preferring the smallest scientifically important effect over an unshrunk pilot estimate or a generic convention.
3. Match the calculation to the planned analysis. Use a closed-form method only for a supported standard design; otherwise use simulation with the same data-generating structure and model planned for the study.
4. Calculate sample size for 80% and 90% power and report whether values are per group, per cluster, or total.
5. Adjust explicitly for unequal allocation, clustering, repeated measurements, multiplicity, dropout, and unusable samples where relevant.
6. Produce sensitivity analyses and power curves over plausible effect sizes and sample sizes. For simulations, report the seed, number of replicates, and Monte Carlo confidence interval.
7. Recommend a planning range rather than a falsely precise single number, and list every assumption that a statistician or study team must verify.

Save power-curve figures as PNG, the complete scenario table as CSV, and a reproducible Markdown report in the sandbox. Summarize the defensible sample-size range, main sensitivity drivers, unresolved inputs, and saved paths in chat.

name: ANOVA / Group Comparisons
description: One-way, two-way, or repeated-measures ANOVA
prompt:
Compare the supplied groups for factor(s) {factors} and outcome {outcome}.

1. Establish the scientific contrast/estimand, independent experimental unit, factors, nesting, repeated measurements and covariates from the study design. Inspect sample sizes, balance and missingness. Independence is a design property, not something a normality test establishes.
2. Choose a model that preserves the design: ordinary one-/multi-factor ANOVA for suitable independent errors; Welch for an appropriate independent one-way unequal-variance comparison; repeated-measures or mixed-effects models for within-unit/correlated data. Use design-matched robust or permutation methods where justified. Kruskal-Wallis applies only to independent one-way groups and is not a generic replacement for repeated-measures or factorial ANOVA. Ask only for missing design information that changes the inference.
3. Check the chosen model's residuals and relevant assumptions; do not select a method solely by Shapiro/Levene p-values. Handle sphericity/covariance assumptions where applicable and report exclusions/missing-data decisions.
4. Report the chosen test's actual statistic and degrees of freedom (F, H or other as applicable), effect estimates in interpretable units, uncertainty and exact p-values. Do not force F-statistics or eta-squared onto an unrelated test.
5. Estimate prespecified contrasts and justified follow-up comparisons, using multiplicity control and a procedure compatible with the model (Tukey only when its assumptions apply). Distinguish exploratory comparisons from planned ones; interpret interactions before marginal effects.
6. Plot distributions or model estimates with clearly defined uncertainty and sample sizes; show paired structure where relevant.
